_comment: SINGLE SOURCE OF TRUTH for the Phase-2 cross-implementation survey. Every figure, table and slide is generated from this file. Add an entry per implementation as it is audited; nothing downstream needs editing. Every value here has been independently verified against source and/or captured measurement -- do not add a value that has not been.

_schema.verified: source | live | source+live -- how the answer was established

q1.quote: an endpoint MUST immediately reset the congestion controller and round-trip time estimator for the new path to initial values

q2.short: Uses path-validation RTT as the new path's initial RTT?
q2.quote: A connection MAY use the delay between sending a PATH_CHALLENGE and receiving a PATH_RESPONSE to set the initial RTT for a new path

q3.short: Excludes old-path ACKs from new-path state?
q3.quote: Packets sent on the old path MUST NOT contribute to congestion control or RTT estimation for the new path

implementations.name: picoquic
implementations.path_model: one path object; migration attaches a new address tuple
implementations.initial_cwnd_effective_note: picoquic sizes its windows from the NEGOTIATED path MTU, not from the 1536 constant. The send size on this testbed is 1424 B, so the window a reset would actually assign is 10 x 1424 = 14,240 B. Both values are treated as reset-shaped when discriminating.
implementations.min_cwnd_formula: PICOQUIC_CWIN_MINIMUM = 2 x MTU = 2 x 1424 (2 x 1536 = 3,072 B by the constant)

q1.mechanism: congestion state belongs to the path object, which is reused; a new address tuple is attached to it
q1.evidence: reset notification has 7 handlers and 0 callers; live, across 5/5 IP-changing migrations ZERO samples took the initial window (15,360 B by the constant, 14,240 B effective at the negotiated 1424 B send size). The window instead fell BELOW both to a minimum of 2,848-8,608 B -- the loss floor, reached ~110 ms after migration with 42-58 packets lost -- which is a loss cascade, not a reset.

q2.mechanism: implemented at frames.c:4943 but gated on !rtt_is_initialized, which is false for the primary path
q2.evidence: code present, never fires in single-path migration

q3.mechanism: no old/new path attribution for ACK-derived samples
q3.evidence: Two independent observations. (a) In the STEP-DOWN experiment (run_topup_and_stepdown.sh, path B 20 Mbit/60 ms) our own compliant reset was re-seeded to 20.3 ms -- the OLD path's RTT -- just 1.8 ms after being cleared. (b) In the five stock repetitions at 20/40 ms, srtt still read 24.7-30.2 ms on the first sample after migrating to a 40 ms path, converging to ~40.3 ms only after about a second. Note the 60 ms figure belongs to (a) alone; the standard operating point uses a 40 ms new path.

live.operating_point: 20 Mbit both paths; path A 20 ms and path B 40 ms one-way netem on the down direction, so true RTTs are ~20 ms and ~40 ms; tbf burst 3200 B; 50 MB transfer; migration at 5 s. This is the Phase-2 standard operating point, identical to the other four implementations.
live.migration_verified: IP change 10.0.1.1 -> 10.0.3.1 with the port UNCHANGED, in 5/5 repetitions, confirmed from the server qlog addr_from/addr_to fields rather than from client stdout. An IP change is NOT covered by the RFC 9000 s9.4 port-only exemption, so the requirement is fully engaged.
live.cwnd_before_definition: the LAST sample before the path-challenge window
live.cwnd_after_definition: the MINIMUM within the migration window and the second following it
live.discriminator: A reset assigns the initial window EXACTLY -- 15,360 B by picoquic's constant, or 14,240 B from the negotiated 1424 B send size. ZERO samples took either value in any of the five repetitions. The window instead fell BELOW both, reaching exactly 2,848 B (= 2 x 1424 = PICOQUIC_CWIN_MINIMUM) in 2 of 5 reps, about 110 ms after the migration window and alongside 42-58 lost packets. A window below the initial value cannot have been produced BY a reset; that is a loss cascade bottoming out at the floor.
live.rtt_reflects: the old path immediately after migration, converging to the new path over roughly one second
live.rtt_detail: srtt 23.4-27.0 ms before migration on the 20 ms path A; 24.7-30.2 ms on the first sample after the migration window, still near path A rather than path B's 40 ms; 40.22-40.44 ms one second later; 40.2-41.0 ms at end of transfer. A compliant implementation would have cleared the estimator to its 250 ms initial RTT and re-measured the new path.
live._correction_2026_08_11: An earlier write-up described the superseded run as 'cwnd flat at 241,174 B across the migration'. That is WRONG and must not be repeated. Re-derived from the trace: the window declined 241,174 -> 146,592 -> 123,888 B through ordinary loss events. The CLAIM was unaffected -- it never approached the initial window -- but it was not flat, and saying so overstated the evidence.
live._supersedes_2026_08_12: These five repetitions replace the single Phase-1 repetition, restoring parity with the other four. The superseded run used 50 Mbit rather than the Phase-2 standard 20 Mbit and so was not directly comparable. It is retained at results/raw/_task2_verify/naive/; its figures were cwnd 241,174 -> 123,888 B, reset_observed false -- the same conclusion.
live._correction_2026_08_12_rtt: The superseded entry recorded new_path_true_rtt_ms = 60.0 with first_post_migration_rtt_ms = 20.3. The 60 ms figure was WRONG for that experiment: it belongs to the step-down scenario (testbed/scenarios/run_topup_and_stepdown.sh, path B 20 Mbit/60 ms), which is where the Q3 contamination evidence came from, and it had been copied into the live block by mistake. The task2_verify shaping logs record delay=20ms on path A and delay=40ms on path B, and that arm's own qlog settles at 41.9 ms after migration.
live._correction_2026_08_12_parser: The verdict line in analysis/parse_qlog.py tested `min_cwnd <= INITIAL * 1.05`, i.e. 'at or BELOW the initial window', and printed RESET OCCURRED. That is wrong and it fired on all five of these repetitions: a window BELOW the initial value cannot have been set by a reset, since a reset assigns the initial value exactly. The test now requires an exact hit and names the loss-cascade case separately. The defect was latent at 50 Mbit, where the cascade never reached the floor.

implementations.notes: Scope: single-path (non-multipath) operation only. With multipath enabled, picoquic_create_path() does produce fresh state.

implementations.name: quic-go

q1.mechanism: explicit reset: MigratedPath() replaces the congestion controller with a new object and resets RTT to a fixed 100 ms
q1.evidence: 2 live call sites (connection.go:915 client, :1295 server reactive); live cwnd peaks 274,025-280,414 -> exactly 40,960 B in 5/5 runs

q2.mechanism: initialRTT is used only as PATH_CHALLENGE probe backoff; ResetForPathMigration always seeds a fixed DefaultInitialRTT
q2.evidence: client logs a measured 40.7 ms probe RTT, then resets to 100 ms

q3.mechanism: structural: DeclareLost sets packets[idx] = nil and the ACK-matching iterator skips nil, so old-path packets are permanently unmatchable
q3.evidence: first post-migration RTT 40.4-40.8 ms on a 40 ms path across 5 runs

live._correction_2026_08_11: History, kept so the numbers are traceable: originally reported as n=4 with a 279,456 B pre-migration window. That was wrong -- the original run's server_metrics.csv had been OVERWRITTEN by later repeats because the trial script hardcodes its output directory, leaving only 3 retained reps. RESOLVED 2026-08-11 by re-running 5 fresh repetitions through _build/quicgo_repeat2.sh, which parses and archives each rep before the next. Current figures are from those 5: peaks 274,025-280,414 -> exactly 40,960 in 5/5, first post-migration RTT 40.4-40.8 ms on a 40 ms path.

implementations.notes: No multipath in the codebase, so a single migration code path and no scoping caveat. addrsEqual compares IP AND port, so it resets on any address change -- it does not take the RFC's port-only leniency.

implementations.name: quiche
implementations.path_model: per-path objects, each with its own Recovery

reset_hook.name: on_connection_migration()
reset_hook.hook_comment: Called when connection migrates and cwnd needs to be reset

q1.mechanism: fresh state by construction: migrating creates a new Path, and Path::new builds a new Recovery at the initial window. Nothing is reset.
q1.evidence: live cwnd 654,900 -> exactly 12,000 B in 5/5 runs; on_path_change() only runs loss detection on the OLD path

q2.mechanism: DEFAULT_INITIAL_RTT = 333 ms is always used; no RTT reference near PathResponse handling
q2.evidence: client logs cwnd=12000 rtt=333ms at cutover, immediately after measuring a 40.6 ms probe RTT

q3.mechanism: structural: per-path Recovery; ACKs routed via paths.get_mut(recv_pid)
q3.evidence: across 5/5 runs path A min_rtt 20.27-20.53 ms and path B min_rtt 40.21-40.24 ms, tracked separately and correctly

implementations.notes: Its qlog does NOT tag metrics with a path id (0 of 98,369 events), so the time series is a union over paths -- per-path evidence comes from path_stats instead. Untested edge case: migrating BACK to a previously-used path reuses that Path object, which retains its old congestion state.

implementations.name: msquic

reset_hook.name: QuicCongestionControlReset()
reset_hook.note: reachable, but only from the OBSERVING side

q1.mechanism: the observer resets; the initiator does not. QuicPathSetActive resets connection-wide congestion control unless the change is port-only, but the client's own QUIC_PARAM_CONN_LOCAL_ADDRESS handler mutates Paths[0] in place and never calls it.
q1.evidence: SOURCE is the load-bearing evidence: QuicPathSetActive (path.c:312) calls QuicCongestionControlReset while the QUIC_PARAM_CONN_LOCAL_ADDRESS handler (connection.c:6426+) does not. Live server side confirms the reset: cwnd 1,481,740-1,484,569 -> exactly 12,200 B in 5/5 reps, rebind=0 in every server log.
q1.evidence_strength_caveat: The client-side half is only CORROBORATED, not proven, by the live data. In a download the client sent 389,341 bytes total of which just 16 were stream bytes -- it is ACK-only, so its congestion window was never the binding constraint and a flat value is what you would expect whether or not a reset occurred. Do NOT present 'client cwnd flat at 96,290 B' as decisive evidence of no-reset; cite the source instead.

q2.mechanism: PATH_RESPONSE handling calls QuicPathSetValid, which touches validation/allowance/MTU only; PathValidationStartTime is used solely for probe timeout
q2.evidence: server srtt seeded to exactly QUIC_INITIAL_RTT (333,000 us) after migration

q3.mechanism: RTT IS excluded by path id (NewLargestAckDifferentPath gates the RTT update at loss_detection.c:1502), but bytes-acked are not: QUIC_ACK_EVENT carries no PathId field, and loss_detection.c:1206 hardcodes Paths[0] with an in-source comment '// TODO - Correct?'
q3.evidence: loss_detection.c:1439 computes the gate; :1502 uses it; the QUIC_ACK_EVENT struct in congestion_control.h has no path field at all

live.rtt_reflects: neither - stuck at the initial default

rtt_stuck.detail: post-migration the server's smoothed RTT stays at exactly 333,000 us and min_rtt at the UINT32_MAX sentinel for every one of ~3,800 samples per rep, across ~20 s. It never recovers a real measurement of the new path.
rtt_stuck.consequence: the sender paces on an RTT ~8x the true 40 ms path; throughput ~13 Mbit/s where quic-go achieved ~19 Mbit/s on the same 20 Mbit testbed
rtt_stuck.caveat: read via QUIC_PARAM_CONN_STATISTICS_V2. An alternative explanation is that the path swap in QuicPathSetActive leaves the polled field stale rather than the estimator being genuinely stuck. Distinguishing these needs an instrumented build - NOT yet done.
rtt_stuck.mechanism_status: UNEXPLAINED - do not attribute a cause
rtt_stuck._correction_2026_08_11: An earlier write-up attributed this to the Q3 RTT gate being 'so strict that the estimator never re-opens'. That attribution is NOT supported. path.c:29 assigns each new path a fresh incrementing ID (Path->ID = Connection->NextPathId++), and QuicPathSetActive swaps the path structs so Paths[0] carries the new ID; packets sent after migration should therefore carry a matching PathId and the gate should open. Why it apparently does not is unknown. The OBSERVATION (5/5 reps, ~3,800 samples each, srtt pinned at 333,000 us and min_rtt at UINT32_MAX for ~20 s) stands on its own and should be reported as an observation only.

implementations.notes: Fourth distinct architecture: congestion control is connection-wide while RTT is per-path. QuicPathSetActive deliberately implements the RFC 9000 s9.4 port-only exemption (UdpPortChangeOnly) - the only surveyed stack to do so on purpose. No usable qlog on Linux (its only qlog code is a Windows ETW post-processor), so instrumentation was stdout tracing plus polling QUIC_PARAM_CONN_STATISTICS_V2; bytes_in_flight unavailable. One rep in five crashed the client with SIGABRT after a stale packet to the old address caused a reactive re-promotion (rebind=1) fighting the just-completed migration - characterised from logs, not root-caused.

implementations.name: ngtcp2
implementations.path_model: connection-wide congestion state, reset wholesale on any path change
implementations.cc_selectable_note: reno, cubic and bbr all implement the ngtcp2_cc interface
implementations.initial_cwnd_formula: min(10 x 1200, max(2 x 1200, 14720)) = 12000 -- the RFC 9002 s7.2 formula implemented exactly

reset_hook.name: conn_reset_congestion_state() -> cc.reset
reset_hook.call_site_breakdown: 6188 conn_recv_path_response (observer, validation success); 8879 and 8992 conn_recv_non_probing_pkt_on_new_path (observer, reactive); 13892 ngtcp2_conn_initiate_immediate_migration (client). The other two are unrelated to migration: 5183 conn_on_path_validation_failed (fallback) and 5602 conn_on_retry.

q1.mechanism: explicit and symmetric: conn_reset_congestion_state() resets cwnd AND the RTT estimator, then dispatches the algorithm's own cc.reset. It fires on BOTH endpoints -- the client at ngtcp2_conn.c:13892 inside initiate_immediate_migration, and the observer at :6188 when path validation promotes a different path.
q1.evidence: conn_reset_conn_stat_cc (ngtcp2_conn.c:906) sets latest_rtt=0, min_rtt=UINT64_MAX, smoothed_rtt=initial_rtt, rttvar=initial_rtt/2, first_rtt_sample_ts=UINT64_MAX, bytes_in_flight=0 and recomputes cwnd from ngtcp2_cc_compute_initcwnd

q2.mechanism: conn_recv_path_response (ngtcp2_conn.c:6154) validates the challenge and promotes the path; it never touches the RTT estimator. The reset seeds smoothed_rtt from the configured initial_rtt setting instead.
q2.evidence: no RTT reference anywhere in PATH_RESPONSE handling

q3.mechanism: a packet-number watermark -- a third distinct mechanism. ngtcp2_rtb_reset_cc_state sets rtb->cc_pkt_num to the next packet number to be sent, and rtb.h:181 documents it as 'the smallest packet number that is contributed to congestion control'. Guards at rtb.c:183, 470 and 923 test pkt_num >= cc_pkt_num, so every packet sent before the migration is excluded from congestion accounting.
q3.evidence: ngtcp2_rtb.c:1477-1480 plus the three guard sites

implementations.notes: Live measurement OBTAINED 2026-08-11 after fixing the build. Root cause of the earlier failure: an interrupted build had left ZERO-BYTE object files and binaries, which ninja then treated as up to date and refused to regenerate ('no work to do' while examples/ptlsclient was 0 bytes). Deleting every zero-byte artefact and rebuilding produced working binaries. Driving the migration needed one more step: ngtcp2's example client exposes --change-local-addr but not a target address -- change_local_addr() (examples/client.cc:1305) asks the ROUTING TABLE which local address reaches the server, which in this testbed returns path A again, i.e. a port-only change that RFC 9000 s9.4 exempts. The trial therefore flips ns_client's main-table route to path B a quarter-second before the timer fires, so the client genuinely binds 10.0.3.1. That also models a real handover more faithfully than an API call would. Confirmed in every rep by the client's own log line 'Local address is now [10.0.3.1]:<port>'. Notable: its RTT reset sets rttvar = initial_rtt/2, matching RFC 9002 Appendix A.3 exactly, where picoquic's own convention uses 0; and it computes its initial window from the exact RFC 9002 s7.2 formula.

cross_cutting_findings.title: Two of the five ship a migration-reset hook that nothing calls
cross_cutting_findings.detail: picoquic's picoquic_congestion_notification_reset has 7 handlers and 0 callers. quiche's on_connection_migration(), commented 'Called when connection migrates and cwnd needs to be reset', has 0 callers and one empty implementation. The other three are reachable: quic-go's MigratedPath() has 2 call sites, msquic's QuicCongestionControlReset() has 2, and ngtcp2's conn_reset_congestion_state() has 6, four of them migration-related. Independent codebases, different languages, the same dead-hook pattern in two of them.

cross_cutting_findings.title: Every implementation reaches its answer by a different mechanism
cross_cutting_findings.detail: quic-go replaces its controller explicitly; quiche is compliant by construction because per-path state means a new path is born at the initial window; picoquic fails because its path object -- and therefore its congestion state -- is reused; msquic is connection-wide for congestion and per-path for RTT, so the observing endpoint resets while the migrating one does not; ngtcp2 is connection-wide too but resets wholesale at BOTH ends and excludes old-path packets with a packet-number watermark. Five implementations, five architectures, five different routes to the answer.

cross_cutting_findings.title: The RFC 9002 §6.2.2 initial-RTT option is universally unused
cross_cutting_findings.detail: All five implementations perform the path-validation round trip, and not one uses the resulting measurement. quic-go and quiche were each caught measuring a ~40 ms probe RTT and then seeding a fixed default (100 ms and 333 ms). msquic seeds exactly its 333 ms default too. ngtcp2's PATH_RESPONSE handler never touches the RTT estimator; its reset seeds smoothed_rtt from the configured initial_rtt setting instead. picoquic is the one partial exception and still does not use it: the code EXISTS at frames.c:4943 but is gated on !rtt_is_initialized, which is false for the primary path, so it never fires in single-path migration.

cross_cutting_findings.title: Compliance is not binary: two implementations required new answer categories
cross_cutting_findings.detail: msquic cannot be scored yes/no on either MUST. For Q1 the answer is ASYMMETRIC -- the observing endpoint resets, the migrating endpoint does not -- so the same connection is simultaneously compliant and non-compliant depending on which end you ask. For Q3 the answer is SPLIT: RTT samples are correctly excluded by path id, but bytes-acked reach the congestion controller unfiltered, because QUIC_ACK_EVENT carries no path id at all and loss_detection.c:1206 hardcodes Paths[0] under an in-source comment reading '// TODO - Correct?'.

cross_cutting_findings.title: In msquic the sender's RTT estimator never recovers after a migration
cross_cutting_findings.detail: Across 5/5 repetitions and roughly 3,800 samples each, the server's smoothed RTT remained at exactly its 333 ms initial default and min_rtt at the UINT32_MAX sentinel for the ~20 s following migration -- it never once measured the new path, whose true RTT was 40 ms. Achieved throughput was ~13 Mbit/s where quic-go reached ~19 Mbit/s on the same 20 Mbit link. Ironically the endpoint that complies with §9.4 ends up with a permanently broken estimate while the endpoint that does not comply keeps a working one.
cross_cutting_findings.status: observed 5/5; needs an instrumented build to separate a genuinely stuck estimator from a stale polled field

cross_cutting_findings.title: Partial compliance with §9.4 is worse than ignoring it
cross_cutting_findings.detail: Implementing the reset (2nd paragraph) without old-path sample exclusion (1st paragraph) took transfer completion from 5/5 to 0/15 in our own picoquic patch. Stale old-path ACKs re-seed the freshly cleared estimator, pacing slow start ~3x too fast for the new path.
